prompt.context: Our client is a large financial services firm with multiple locations around the world. Part of their service offering includes a 24-hour helpline. The client has their call centers in New York and Paris. The client has recently acquired a small firm (Firm B) in order to expand its reach in a particular geography. Firm B provides a subset of the services and has its call center located in the Philippines.
prompt.question: The client has asked us to determine its strategy going forward for handling customer calls. In particular, they want us to look into the call center operations. The client wants any proposed solution to be cash neutral by the end of year 2 and is not flexible on this requirement.

clarifying_info.q: What services does the client provide?
clarifying_info.a: The client provides the full range of financial services for individuals and small organizations.

clarifying_info.q: How long has the acquired firm been operating?
clarifying_info.a: The acquired firm (Firm B) was started 5 years ago and is still run by the original founders.

clarifying_info.q: What are the hiring requirements for call center employees?
clarifying_info.a: New employees are college graduates with basic knowledge of financial services and products. Fluency in English and several European languages is required.

It is very difficult to lay off employees in the Paris location — significant costs will be incurred. The Philippines government encourages investment in the country, so significant tax advantages are possible.

clarifying_info.q: Are the call centers currently operating at capacity?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, all three call centers are currently operating at full capacity.

clarifying_info.q: Is there space and infrastructure to expand the Philippines facility?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, currently there is space and infrastructure available to expand. Assume overhead is variable in this case.

exhibits.title: Call center performance – FY2010
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the three call centers (New York, Paris, Philippines) across four metrics: calls per year, employee cost per year ($), overhead cost per year ($), and number of employees.

framework: Options analysis: (1) No changes — maintain all 3 call centers; (2) Close Firm B's Philippines call center and route calls to NY or Paris; (3) Consolidate to a single location (likely Philippines given cost advantage)
Company / operational comparison: Compare services offered at the 3 call centers, evaluate performance metrics (cost per call, calls per rep, total cost), assess capacity and scalability
Integration and one-time costs: Severance for NY and Paris employees, cost to expand Philippines facility, hiring and training costs in Philippines

Qualitative / outsourcing-specific concerns: Employment regulations (especially Paris layoffs), quality of service and language requirements, reputational risk, organizational culture of acquired Firm B, public opinion
Financial feasibility: Client requires cash-neutral solution by end of year 2 — test each option against this constraint
Implementation plan: Timeline for knowledge transfer, talent acquisition, infrastructure build-out, and best-practice transfer

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the total current cost and the efficiency (calls per employee per year and cost per call) of each call center.
questions.guidance: Strong answers will compute total cost per location, derive calls/employee/year and cost/call for each site, and identify that Philippines is the cheapest per call ($6) but least efficient per employee (4,000 calls/employee vs. 8,000 in NY).

math.setup: Total cost = (employee cost per year × employees) + overhead. Calls/employee = calls per year ÷ employees. Cost/call = total cost ÷ calls per year.
math.answer: Total current cost = $9.6M. Calls/employee/year: NY 8,000; Paris 6,667; Philippines 4,000. Cost/call: NY $7; Paris $9; Philippines $6. Philippines is cheapest per call but handles only half the volume per employee compared to NY.

questions.prompt: If we consolidate all calls to the Philippines at current efficiency (4,000 calls/employee/year), how many additional employees are needed and what is the new total operating cost? Does this meet the client's two-year breakeven requirement, given a one-time investment cost of $5M?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate headcount needed for total call volume of 1.3M calls, derive new operating cost, compare savings vs. one-time cost, and check against the two-year breakeven constraint.

math.setup: Total calls to handle = 600,000 + 400,000 + 300,000 = 1,300,000. At current Philippines efficiency of 4,000 calls/employee, headcount required = 1,300,000 ÷ 4,000. New operating cost = headcount × ($20,000 employee cost + overhead per employee). One-time cost = $5M (severance for NY and Paris + Philippines expansion).
steps: Net after 2 years: $3,600,000 − $5,000,000 = −$1,400,000 (not cash neutral by year 2)
math.answer: New operating cost = $7.8M, saving $1.8M/year. However, the $5M one-time cost yields only $3.6M in two-year savings, leaving a $1.4M shortfall. The consolidation at current Philippines efficiency does NOT meet the two-year breakeven requirement.

questions.prompt: Can we make the Philippines consolidation feasible within the two-year constraint? What happens if Philippines achieves the same efficiency as New York (8,000 calls/employee/year)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should independently explore improving Philippines efficiency as the lever. Strong answer transfers best practices from NY to Philippines, recalculates headcount and cost, and verifies breakeven.

math.setup: If Philippines achieves 8,000 calls/employee/year: headcount = 1,300,000 ÷ 8,000. Overhead doubles due to better equipment (assume $1/call × 1.3M calls = $1.3M × 2 = $2.6M).
steps: Net after 2 years: $7,600,000 − $5,000,000 = +$2,600,000 (cash positive by year 2)
math.answer: With Philippines at NY-level efficiency, total operating cost drops to $5.8M, saving $3.8M/year. Two-year savings of $7.6M exceed the $5M one-time cost, meeting the cash-neutral-by-year-2 requirement with $2.6M to spare.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative risks and concerns should the client consider before proceeding with consolidation to the Philippines?

categories.name: People & Talent
ideas: Can sufficient qualified talent be hired in the Philippines within 3–6 months?
Language requirements (English + European languages) may limit the talent pool
Knowledge transfer from NY/Paris to Philippines may have gaps
Employee morale during transition; possible attrition at all sites

categories.name: Service Quality
ideas: Customer satisfaction impact if service quality declines during transition
Customers may notice change in accent or cultural familiarity
More complex financial products may be harder to support offshore

categories.name: Regulatory & Legal
ideas: Significant severance costs and legal constraints for Paris layoffs
Need to model true all-in one-time cost including Paris severance
Philippines tax incentives could reduce one-time investment cost

categories.name: Organizational / Cultural
ideas: Firm B was founded 5 years ago and is still run by original founders — culture clash risk
Integration of acquired firm's processes and systems with client's operations
Change management for the acquiring firm's employees being let go

categories.name: Reputational & Competitive
ideas: Public backlash from large-scale offshoring announcement
Competitors could use this news to attract dissatisfied customers
Brand perception tied to service quality of call center

recommendation: Recommend consolidating all call center operations to the Philippines, contingent on successfully transferring best practices from NY to achieve 8,000 calls/employee/year within 3–6 months
This achieves cash neutrality well within the two-year requirement (estimated +$2.6M net by end of year 2) and reduces steady-state operating costs from $9.6M to $5.8M annually

There is no single right answer — an alternative recommendation to maintain multiple locations is acceptable if the candidate adequately justifies it on qualitative grounds (e.g., language requirements, service quality, regulatory constraints)
risks: Capacity risk: scaling Philippines headcount by more than 200% (from 75 to ~160 employees) in a short timeframe strains recruitment, training, and infrastructure
Service quality risk: customers may notice a difference in service, and competitors could exploit any perceived quality decline
Knowledge transfer risk: best-practice transfer may take longer than 3–6 months, delaying efficiency gains and threatening the breakeven timeline
Paris severance risk: actual costs of laying off Paris employees may be higher than the $5M estimate due to strict French labor laws
Organizational risk: Firm B is founder-run; integrating its culture and operations with the larger firm may create friction
next_steps: Conduct a detailed infrastructure assessment for Philippines expansion (office space, IT, telephony)
Begin talent acquisition planning immediately; identify language-proficient candidates
Design a structured knowledge-transfer program from NY/Paris to Philippines with measurable milestones
Engage legal counsel in France and New York to finalize severance cost estimates
Develop a customer communication and change management plan to protect brand reputation during the transition
